title: Legendary Artist Luis Felipe Noé (1933-2025) Dies
text:
Argentine art has lost a true icon. The recent passing of Luis Felipe Noé, affectionately known as “ Yuyo ,” marks the end of an era for those familiar with the revolutionary work of this legendary artist. This article explores the life, career, and lasting impact of Luis Felipe Noé, offering a thorough look at his contributions to Argentine and international art.
Luis Felipe “Yuyo” Noé, Argentine Art Icon, Dies at 91 A towering figure in Argentine art, Luis Felipe noé, known affectionately as “yuyo,” passed away at the age of 91, succumbing to health complications. He was surrounded by family and close associates in his final moments.
Noé remained active in his studio until recently, his vitality undiminished as he engaged with the art world, attending colleagues’ openings and cultural events.
A legacy of Reinvention Noé emerged as one of ArgentinaS most meaningful painters in the latter half of the 20th century. From his early landscapes of northern Argentina in the 1950s to his pivotal role in the Otra Figuración movement alongside artists like De la Vega, Macció, and Deira, Noé consistently pushed boundaries.This movement placed Argentine art at the forefront of international avant-garde trends, all while maintaining a distinct local identity.
Throughout his career, Noé repeatedly reinvented himself, challenging established artistic norms.
He blurred the lines between figuration and abstraction. He explored the interplay of drawing and painting. He questioned the relationship between plane and volume. He investigated the tension between the static and the dynamic. His artistic curiosity drove him to synthesize painting with reflections on the state of the world. He was also a pioneer of artistic installations in the mid-1960s.
Theoretical Contributions and writings Beyond his painting, Noé was a respected essayist and theorist. His seminal work, Antiestética , will mark its 50th anniversary of its first edition in 2025. He also authored other influential books, including The art in question (2001), a dialog with Horacio Zabala, and And not written about what is called Arte (2007). His final book, Assume chaos – in life and art , published last year, served as his comprehensive theoretical and personal testament.
Noé’s influence extended to education, where he mentored generations of artists, many of whom he actively promoted.
Embracing Chaos: Noé’s artistic Philosophy Noé’s artistic vision was deeply intertwined with the concept of chaos. He explicitly formulated the “assumption of chaos,” exploring the idea of “Chaos as a structure” in his writings. This philosophy permeated his work, influencing his compositions and themes.
One of the chapters of his Antiestética It is titled “Chaos as a structure.”
He drew inspiration from a wide range of sources, including aesthetic experiences, politics, history, and contemporary Argentine society.
Key Moments and Influences A pivotal moment in Noé’s career was his nine-month stay in New York in 1964, made possible by the Di Tella award. He returned to new York the following year after receiving a Guggenheim scholarship.
Between 1968 and 1974, Noé temporarily stepped back from his artistic practise, focusing on political and cultural engagement. He even managed a bar called “the barbarian,” which became a hub in Buenos Aires.
The onset of the dictatorship in 1976 forced Noé into exile with his wife, Nora Murphy, and their children, Paula and Gaspar. Thay lived in Paris for 11 years.
A visit to the Amazon in the mid-1980s profoundly impacted his work, leading him to revisit and expand upon the installation art he had explored in the 1960s.
Venice Biennale and Later Career A significant moment in the recognition of Noé’s work in the 21st century was his selection as the artist representing Argentina at the 2009 Venice Biennale. This event provided a platform for monumental works, including The static speed , measuring 11 meters wide by 3 meters high, and the polyptych We are understanding ourselves , comprised of 15 paintings.
The curator for the argentine shipment to the 2009 Venice Biennial stated, They were very happy and unforgettable moments for Noah, even though not only for him.
following the Biennale, his work toured Argentina in 2010.
Recent Exhibitions and Themes Recent major exhibitions of Noé’s work include “Prospective look” (National Museum of Fine Arts, Buenos Aires, 2017) and “Quebrada Vision” (Mar del Plata Museum, 2023/24), both curated by Cecilia Ivanche.
In his later years, Noé’s works explored themes of farewell and reflection, often incorporating fragmented imagery and text. His approach combined chance and intention, resulting in dynamic and thought-provoking compositions.
One of the strong characteristics is the anticipatory fragmentation of the pictorial field in their works, which were in turn accounting for the process of fragmentation of the subject contemporaries and of certain effects of technology.
Foundation Statement The Luis Felipe Noé foundation released a statement following his death:
With deep regret, from the Luis Felipe Noé Foundation we reported the death of Luis Felipe Noé, a basic artist whose work and thought deeply transformed Argentine and Latin American art.
Luis Felipe Noé Foundation
The foundation, established in 2019, aims to preserve and promote Noé’s legacy.
We celebrate his life, his inexhaustible creative impulse and his sharp look as a way of understanding the world. His legacy lasts in each work, in each word, in every gesture that invited to think and to create. From the Foundation, we appreciate your teachings and the possibility of opening this shared path, and we reaffirm our commitment to your thinking: we will continue to honor your memory in each action of our existence, because in the doing one lives and in the doing it grows.
Luis Felipe Noé Foundation
Funeral Arrangements A public viewing will be held this Thursday, April 10, at the Buenos Aires Legislature from 9:30 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The funeral will take place on Friday at 11:00 a.m. in the Recoleta cemetery.
